title: Near-field GNSS motion in days 30-365 kept the early postseismic pattern but was 2.5 times the aftershock late-to-early ratio after 22 large shallow earthquakes (2002-2025)
abstract: Question: a prior campaign study found that GNSS postseismic displacement grows later in the first year than aftershock counts after 24 large shallow earthquakes. Does a separate broad process make the late GNSS motion, or does the same source continue with fewer aftershocks? Approach: for the same 24 events, we used 441 Nevada Geodetic Laboratory stations out to 6 rupture radii (R) and computed coseismic, early (day 1-30) and late (day 30-365) displacement vectors, with a placebo 420 days earlier for noise. We wrote the tests before we computed the vectors. Results: at the nearest stations (below 0.5 R where available), late motion along the early direction was a median 1.50 times the early motion (95% CI 1.33-1.69), but the aftershock late-to-early ratio was 0.59; the GNSS ratio was larger in 21 of 22 events (p = 1.5e-4), for onshore and offshore events. The late field was close to a scaled copy of the early field (median k 1.39; unexplained power share 0.06), while the same test separated the early field from the coseismic field (share 0.28, 12 of 12 events). The late-to-early ratio did not change clearly with distance (slope 0.31, CI -0.66 to 0.55, 13 events). A post hoc test with the coseismic field as reference found a gradual broadening of late motion (13 of 14 events), but aftershock ratios did not increase with distance. We also found that the prior step-removal rule used pre-event days for early M6+ steps; the corrected rule removed false late reversals at Iquique and Illapel but did not change the prior conclusion. Conclusion: a separate broad process does not by itself explain the mismatch; near the rupture, a source with nearly the early pattern continues with far fewer aftershocks per unit motion. Limitations: few far stations have a clear early signal; onshore-only stations for offshore ruptures; no physical model; coupling changes can add late motion.

Orange: aftershock excess count in days 30-365 divided by days 1-30 (prior study). GNSS was larger in 21 of 22 events.

Unexplained share of horizontal displacement power for a scaled-copy fit. Blue: late field against the early field. Gray: early field against the coseismic field on the same stations (benchmark of a known source change). Black ticks: noise-only level for the late fit.

A: GNSS late-to-early ratio q per station (|early| >= 3 sigma) and by distance ring, with the pooled aftershock ratio by ring. B: median early and late motion divided by coseismic motion by distance bin (post hoc); late motion grows more with distance.
